question: SQ-LIP-000002
text: How common is lipedema, and who does it affect?
minor_problems: [minor] set: Prevalence figure of about 11% is propagated through citation chains (E7, E11, E13, E15, E16, E22, E25) and E2 is a consensus on the same Brazilian estimate as E1; independence is overstated and P1 and P2 partly twin/tension each other.
[minor] set: Clinic-based proportions (E11, E19, E14, E28, E30) are mixed between P1 and P3; E28 and E14 non-obese/hormonal data scattered across propositions.

[minor] P1: not fully supported; overgeneralized; misplaced ['E11', 'E19'] — suggested: Questionnaire-based and secondary estimates suggest lipedema may affect a sizeable minority of adult women, though true general-population prevalence is uncertain. (Only primary data is one self-reported screening questionnaire (probable lipedema); E2/E3 restate it, E22 and much of E11/E19 repeat a secondary 11% figure. Clinic proportions (15%, 18.8%, 15-17%) are not general-population prevalence. Stronger 'common rather than rare' wording is in tension with E23/E24 (lower or underestimated figures).)

[minor] P2: two ideas (Variation is shown (1:72,000 to about 11%). Underdiagnosis and lack of biomarker/ICD code are supported (E24, E7); 'validated diagnostic criteria' is slightly beyond 'no validated biomarker'. Could cite E14/E13 for underdiagnosis.)

[minor] P3: not fully supported — suggested: Lipedema is found in a minority to sizeable share of patients seen in vein, lymphology or limb-swelling clinics, depending on selection. ('Frequently' is vague: 7.7% in vein clinic, 9/250 (3.6%) in lymphedema series, 71% in a selected edema cohort. E11 (15%, 18.8%) and E19 (15-17%) belong here rather than P1.)

[minor] P6: misplaced ['E21', 'E9', 'E6', 'E28'] (E15 finding is mainly a review statement. Puberty onset 57% (E21), 62.2% adolescent (E9), 63.8% hormonal (E28), 49% puberty (E14) are stronger and sit elsewhere. Menopause rests only on E15.)

[minor] P7: misplaced ['E21', 'E8'] — suggested: A positive family history is frequently reported in lipedema, which may point to a heritable component. (E16 and E25 are reviews citing the same figure; E21 (85%) and E8 (72.6%) are primary data placed elsewhere or unused. Familial reporting alone does not establish heritability; 'suggesting' is mild enough.)
[minor] P8: misplaced ['E14', 'E13'] (Well supported by E20, E21, E6. E14 (77% undiagnosed), E13 (93% unrecognized) and E19 would strengthen it.)

[minor] P9: misplaced ['E28'] (E18 is about edema/lymphedema by BMI and E13 a single case; the best support is E28 (39% non-obese) which is not placed here. E26 as contradicting is a fair, older review claim.)

propositions.statement: Lipedema is estimated to affect a substantial proportion of adult women, suggesting it is a common rather than rare condition.
propositions.rationale: Questionnaire-based and review-cited prevalence estimates consistently place lipedema among common conditions in adult women.

evidence.finding: Validated online screening questionnaire estimated lipedema prevalence of 12.3% among adult Brazilian women, conservatively about 8.8 million women aged 18-69 with suggestive symptoms.
English version of the same Brazilian study: prevalence 12.3% ± 4% (95% CI) at cut-off 12, extrapolated to about 8.8 million women aged 18-69.
Delphi consensus accepted the statement that lipedema prevalence in Brazil is 12.3% of adult women, though with the lowest agreement among accepted statements (3.78/5; evidence 3.49/5).
Systematic review compiles prevalence of 11% in women, 15% of lymphology clinic patients, 6.5% of children referred as lymphedema, and 18.8% of 843 patients with lower-limb enlargement.
Review estimates lipedema affects about 1 in 9 adult women and notes 15-17% of patients treated for lymphedema have concomitant lipedema.
Surgical cohort background states lipedema affects 11% of women and is often misdiagnosed.

propositions.statement: Lipedema prevalence estimates vary widely and remain uncertain, partly because of underdiagnosis and the lack of validated diagnostic criteria.
propositions.rationale: Reported figures range from very rare to very common, and reviews attribute this to diagnostic limitations.

evidence.finding: Review cites a minimum prevalence of 1:72,000 in the general population, considered an underestimate, versus 39% (9.7% moderate-severe) in a German sample of 62 professional women.
Review gives estimated prevalence of 6-11% in women (worldwide about 10%), considered underestimated due to absent ICD-10 code in the US and no validated diagnostic biomarker.
Review cites an estimated 11% worldwide prevalence in women with acknowledged diagnostic limitation, and states true prevalence and incidence remain poorly defined.

propositions.statement: Lipedema is frequently identified among patients attending vein, lymphology or limb-swelling clinics.
propositions.rationale: Several clinical-setting studies find lipedema in a notable share of patients referred for other leg conditions.

evidence.finding: Lipedema was diagnosed in 7.7% (36/464) of women consulting a vein clinic for mild-to-moderate superficial venous disorder; 39% were non-obese and onset was hormonal in 63.8%.
Among 115 patients with lower-limb edema, lipedema was clinically confirmed in 71%, all women, mean age 38.6, mean BMI 30.5; 77% had no prior diagnosis.
Among 250 lower-extremity lymphedema cases, 9 patients had lipedema with symmetric foot-sparing swelling and negative Stemmer sign, considered a distinct entity.

propositions.statement: Lipedema is reported almost exclusively in women.
propositions.rationale: Reviews and patient samples consistently report female-only or near-exclusively female populations.

evidence.finding: Systematic review of lipedema pathology states it almost exclusively affects females.
Two-case report describes lipedema as primarily affecting women and under-recognized in India with scarce epidemiological data.
Systematic review of 7 lymphoscintigraphy studies: all 311 lipedema patients were women, mean age 47.4 years, mean BMI 32.6.

propositions.statement: Lipedema with the classical phenotype can occur in men, although male cases are rare.
propositions.rationale: Case reports and series document male lipedema while confirming it is much less frequent than in women.

evidence.finding: Five men aged 31-58 with classical phenotype; male lipedema prevalence cited as about 0.2% worldwide; no histopathology.
Case report of a 53-year-old man notes lipedema is less frequent in men than women and weight gain aggravates it in both sexes.

propositions.statement: Lipedema onset or worsening is frequently reported at female hormonal transitions, especially puberty, and also pregnancy and menopause.
propositions.rationale: Multiple cohorts and reviews report onset clustered around hormonal transitions.

evidence.finding: In a US survey of 707 women, mean age 48.6, mean BMI 40.9; onset at puberty in 48.0% and pregnancy in 41.2%.
In 106 female liposuction patients, pubertal onset 58.5%, pregnancy 20.8%, family history 72.6%, upper-limb involvement 61.3%; hypothyroidism, migraine and depression elevated.
Review plus chart review of 46 women: onset typically at puberty, childbirth or menopause, familial aggregation suggesting autosomal dominant inheritance, estimated prevalence 11-15% of adult women.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: Lipedema symptom onset frequently coincides with hormonal life events, particularly puberty, and also pregnancy or menopause.

propositions.statement: A positive family history is frequently reported among people with lipedema, though reported frequencies vary widely.
propositions.rationale: Patient cohorts and reviews report familial clustering in a large share of cases.

evidence.finding: In 360 Italian women, positive family history in 81.2% (289/356): 40.2% maternal, 32.6% paternal, no difference by stage.
In 381 Swiss referral women (mean age 41.9), 49.9% reported family history, 62.2% adolescent onset, 92.1% had comorbidities.
Narrative review cites prevalence of 11-15% of adult women and familial aggregation in up to 60% of cases, suggesting autosomal dominant inheritance.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: A positive family history is frequently reported in lipedema, suggesting a heritable predisposition.

propositions.statement: Lipedema is frequently underrecognised, with diagnosis often delayed for many years after symptom onset.
propositions.rationale: Surveys of patients report long intervals between early onset and diagnosis.

evidence.finding: Swedish national survey: 69% had onset before age 30 but only 1.6% were diagnosed before that age; most frequent diagnosis age 50-59 (34.9%).
In 138 patients, 85% family history, 57% puberty-related onset (median 14.8 years), and median diagnostic delay over 25 years.
In 209 German female liposuction patients, onset at mean age 16 and diagnosis took a mean of 15 years; hypothyroidism 35.9%, depression 23.0%.

propositions.statement: Lipedema is reported in women of normal or low body weight, not only in women with obesity.
propositions.rationale: Several items describe lipedema at normal weight, while one review frames it as a disorder of obese women.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Questionnaire-based and secondary estimates suggest lipedema may affect a sizeable minority of adult women, though true general-population prevalence is uncertain.
verdicts.note: Only primary data is one self-reported screening questionnaire (probable lipedema); E2/E3 restate it, E22 and much of E11/E19 repeat a secondary 11% figure. Clinic proportions (15%, 18.8%, 15-17%) are not general-population prevalence. Stronger 'common rather than rare' wording is in tension with E23/E24 (lower or underestimated figures).

Variation is shown (1:72,000 to about 11%). Underdiagnosis and lack of biomarker/ICD code are supported (E24, E7); 'validated diagnostic criteria' is slightly beyond 'no validated biomarker'. Could cite E14/E13 for underdiagnosis.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Lipedema is found in a minority to sizeable share of patients seen in vein, lymphology or limb-swelling clinics, depending on selection.
verdicts.note: 'Frequently' is vague: 7.7% in vein clinic, 9/250 (3.6%) in lymphedema series, 71% in a selected edema cohort. E11 (15%, 18.8%) and E19 (15-17%) belong here rather than P1.
Consistent with many all-female samples; E29 and E27 are weak but non-contradictory; P5 handles male exceptions.
Small case series and a case report; hedged 'can occur' and 'rare' is adequate. The 0.2% figure is a cited estimate.
E15 finding is mainly a review statement. Puberty onset 57% (E21), 62.2% adolescent (E9), 63.8% hormonal (E28), 49% puberty (E14) are stronger and sit elsewhere. Menopause rests only on E15.

verdicts.suggested_statement: A positive family history is frequently reported in lipedema, which may point to a heritable component.
verdicts.note: E16 and E25 are reviews citing the same figure; E21 (85%) and E8 (72.6%) are primary data placed elsewhere or unused. Familial reporting alone does not establish heritability; 'suggesting' is mild enough.
Well supported by E20, E21, E6. E14 (77% undiagnosed), E13 (93% unrecognized) and E19 would strengthen it.
E18 is about edema/lymphedema by BMI and E13 a single case; the best support is E28 (39% non-obese) which is not placed here. E26 as contradicting is a fair, older review claim.

set_issues.issue: Prevalence figure of about 11% is propagated through citation chains (E7, E11, E13, E15, E16, E22, E25) and E2 is a consensus on the same Brazilian estimate as E1; independence is overstated and P1 and P2 partly twin/tension each other.
Clinic-based proportions (E11, E19, E14, E28, E30) are mixed between P1 and P3; E28 and E14 non-obese/hormonal data scattered across propositions.
